full_judgment: 17. In that case I held that it was the prosecution to prove that bringing of the categories of goods mentioned in section 156(8) into Bangladesh were prohibited and/or restricted and those were brought by any road other than a route declared under section 9 and 10 of the Customs Act. But in the instant case the conviction is made not only under section 156(8) of the Customs Act, 1969 but as well under clause (89) of Sub-section (8) of section 156 of the Act. A close reading of clause (89) of sub-section (8) of section 156 of the Customs Act, 1969 that the burden lies on the accused to offer a lawful excuse for acquisition of possession of, or is in any way concerned in carrying, removing, depositing, harbouring, keeping or concealing, or in any manner dealing with smuggled goods or any goods with respect to which there may be reasonable suspicion that they are smuggled goods. Although in a criminal case the onus is always on the prosecution to prove that the offence was committed by the accused persons but Clause (89) of sub-section (8) of section 156 is an exception of the rule. In this case clause (89) casts a duty on the accused persons to offer a lawful excuse for carrying the goods which are smuggled or regarding which there is reasonable suspicion that they are smuggled goods. Now Lain to see whether in this case the appellants have offered a lawful excuse for carrying the sarees in question. From the evidence on record it appears that the sarees were kept in 29 closed gunny bags and the goods were carried by a public carrier. I can not hold that the accused appellants had any reasonable suspicion about the same to be smuggled goods in that they were kept in closed gunny bags and in absence of any evidence to the effect that the accused suspected those to be smuggled goods the accused disclosed the names of the truck owner and by such disclosure, in my opinion, they have discharged their onus of offering a lawful excuse for carrying the goods which are suspected as smuggled one by the prosecution. In my opinion the driver and the helper of a public carrier discharge their onus of offering a lawful excuse as enjoined upon them under clause (89) of sub-section (8) of section 156 of the Customs Act, 1969, in carrying such goods as soon as they disclose the names of the owner of such carrier. In this case the prosecution failed to secure the arrest of the owners of goods and the truck although the appellant disclosed the name and address of the truck owner who was the best witness to depose regarding the ownership of the sarees and the oil carried in the truck. Certainly it is not the appellants who were the owners of the goods, the owners must be either the owner of the truck or some other person who hired the truck for carrying the goods to Dhaka. It is also seen from the evidence on record that the drums containing palm oil were given to one person. But the prosecution did not also disclose the name of that person. Failure to secure arrest of those persons is the total negligence in discharging his duties by the Investigating Officer (PW 10) in this case. The owner of the truck in which the sarees were carried in closed gunny bags was the best person to know the particulars about the goods and the person to whom the drums were given. Non examination of such material witnesses to prove smuggle raises an adverse presumption against the prosecution in this case taking into consideration the defence suggestion that the sarees were stolen goods and the owners of the same were released from the truck and not arrested by the police and a false case was filed against the appellant to save his service by I.O. This failure on the part of the Investigating Officer to secure arrest of the owner of the truck and withholding of the name of the persons to whom the drums containing palm oil was given fits in with the defence suggestion that the accused were falsely implicated in this case by the Investigation Officer in order to save his job. Thus I am of the opinion that in this case the accused persons arc entitled to the benefit of section 114(g) of the Evidence Act for non-examination of material witnesses. So far as seizure list witness is concerned there was defence suggestion that the witnesses were not present at the place of occurrence from where the truck was seized the place near the Kachpur bridge. This aspect of the defence version has not received due consideration by the Tribunal. This is an important aspect to be considered in this case. This coupled with the statement of PW 10 to the effect that prior to seizure of the truck no information was given to the police station also create sufficient doubt as to the manner and place of arrest of the appellants and seizure of the truck.
